The diagnostic in practice.

Ten anonymised operational contexts. Each case shows the presenting problem, what the evidence revealed, the intervention and the outcome.

Company names are withheld. Metrics and findings shown here are confirmed for publication.

Case-study library

01Multi-site industrial distributionThe OTIF problem was not in the warehouseThe warehouse was absorbing the failure of a promise it had no part in making.60% → 85%Network OTIF · 12 months

Challenge

OTIF sat near 60% across a 16-branch network. Improvement activity had concentrated on picking, despatch and warehouse capacity.

Diagnosis

Promise dates did not use live branch stock and the measure ended at despatch, not customer delivery. Many orders reached branches already late.

Rebuild

Live-stock promise logic, delivery-confirmed OTIF and a daily review of at-risk orders shifted action upstream.

Outcome

OTIF reached 85% within 12 months, without capital investment or a headcount change.

02Branch network inventoryReducing stock without collapsing serviceExcess stock was a rational response to an unreliable replenishment signal.2.4 → 3.6Inventory turns · 14 months

Challenge

Two previous stock-reduction attempts had been abandoned after service deterioration across the branch-and-hub network.

Diagnosis

Actual replenishment took two days longer than the system assumed, while branch forecasts underused local demand history.

Rebuild

Corrected lead-time logic, local demand data and segmented rundown plans replaced a blanket SKU reduction.

Outcome

Inventory turns rose to 3.6 over 14 months while service held and then improved.

03Network restructuringThe branch that looked worst on cost was not the structural problemThe key question was whether underperformance was local or imported from upstream.2 of 3Proposed closures retained

Challenge

Three branches below target on cost, utilisation and customer satisfaction were proposed for consolidation.

Diagnosis

One site was structurally unviable. A second carried centrally generated routing cost. A third had a correctable management gap.

Rebuild

Close one branch, correct routing across the 16-site network and install permanent leadership with a six-month recovery plan.

Outcome

Two branches remained open while the cost and capacity targets that triggered the review were still met.

04Continuous improvement disciplineActivity is not the same as compound improvementThe programme recorded actions as complete before verifying whether the change held.1.27 → 2.0CI maturity · 12 months

Challenge

A national operation’s CI maturity had not moved after six months of workshops and centrally deployed support.

Diagnosis

A sample of 40 completed actions exposed a verification gap: outcomes were not consistently checked after implementation.

Rebuild

Every action received a 30-day and 90-day check, with degraded results returning to root-cause review.

Outcome

CI maturity reached 2.0 within 12 months through stronger verification, not more activity.

05Transformation leadershipEngagement improved when the change made visible sensePeople received instructions and timelines, but not the problem each change was meant to solve.64 → 71Engagement score · 12 months

Challenge

Engagement lagged its benchmark during a multi-year transformation, particularly on direction and confidence in change.

Diagnosis

The logic was clear at leadership level but absent at branch and team level, making beneficial and disruptive changes indistinguishable.

Rebuild

Each change began with the problem, success measure and adjustment route before managers briefed teams.

Outcome

The engagement score reached 71, led by gains in understanding direction and confidence in the programme.

06Value-added technical servicesThe revenue gap was a service-architecture problemThe commercial team was chasing the pipeline; the leakage sat in scheduling and billing.30.5% → 34.6%VAS revenue share · 18 months

Challenge

Value-added-services revenue share had stalled despite sustained sales activity and healthy enquiry and conversion rates.

Diagnosis

VAS bookings lost capacity to core work, while a manual billing handoff missed about 6% of completed jobs.

Rebuild

A separate VAS resource model and automated field-delivery-to-billing trigger closed the post-sale gap.

Outcome

VAS revenue share reached 34.6% over 18 months by fixing the service architecture behind the sale.

07Specialist international mailOperational credibility built the commercial pipelineBuyers needed evidence that the operation could carry the promise before evaluating the proposition.~£20mNew contracted revenue · 36 months

Challenge

Outbound activity in a sophisticated, risk-sensitive buyer segment was generating low engagement.

Diagnosis

Commercial propositions arrived before new contacts could verify operational capability and exception management.

Rebuild

The sequence led with network design, exception capability and delivery evidence, followed by the commercial proposal.

Outcome

The capability-first approach generated approximately £20m in contracted revenue over 36 months.

08International postal logisticsA billing exception was an operations problem finance inheritedData quality failures entered the record at despatch and surfaced later as finance overhead.−30%Billing exceptions · 8 months

Challenge

EDI billing exceptions required a large weekly manual-resolution process owned entirely by finance.

Diagnosis

Missing or incorrect despatch fields and outdated partner tolerances created exceptions before reconciliation began.

Rebuild

Pre-transmission validation addressed data quality at source and bilateral tolerances were reset to the current service mix.

Outcome

Billing exceptions fell 30% within eight months and the manual finance workload reduced proportionally.

09Temperature-controlled pharmaceutical logisticsPassing the KPI while failing the customerThe SLA recorded success even when product-specific temperature evidence triggered quarantine.Near zeroClient quarantines · 3 months

Challenge

Contracted service measures did not explain the client reviews and quarantine decisions following apparently compliant deliveries.

Diagnosis

The SLA omitted product-profile thresholds and two hub operations exceeded the thermal tolerance of the pack type in use.

Rebuild

Product thresholds joined the measurement framework, pack specifications were reviewed and hub dwell gained a maximum window.

Outcome

Client quarantine events fell to near zero within three months of the hub protocol change.

10Current assignment · MedTech companyBuild a baseline the business can defendIn a regulated environment, a reliable baseline is part of the corrective-action evidence.45% → 66%OTIF · 3 months

Challenge

Low OTIF, weak inventory velocity and excess stock required rapid action without compromising regulatory traceability.

Diagnosis

The first step tested how OTIF, stock turns and inventory exposure were defined and segmented by customer, product and supply constraint.

Rebuild

A defensible baseline, focused operating cadence and targeted inventory actions connected each intervention to measurable evidence.

Outcome · first 3 months

  • 45% → 66%OTIF improvement
  • 1.9 → 3.1Stock-turn improvement
  • 10%Inventory released
